content.title: Maintaining Paragraph Unity and Overall Focus
content.overview: Paragraph unity is the principle that every sentence in a paragraph must support a single, clearly defined main idea. On the ACT, you must identify sentences that deviate from this focus and either remove them or revise them to strengthen their connection to the central theme.
learning_objectives: Identify the single main idea of a paragraph in a concise phrase.
Evaluate whether a specific sentence directly supports, explains, or illustrates that main idea.
Apply the Single-Focus Sentence Check to remove or rewrite irrelevant information.
Distinguish between relevant supporting details and distracting 'tangent' information.

sections.title: The Single-Focus Sentence Check
sections.content: To maintain unity, you must first determine the paragraph's 'anchor'—the one clear main idea. Once identified, perform the Single-Focus Sentence Check: evaluate every sentence against that anchor. If a sentence introduces a new topic, a separate debate, or an unrelated detail, it breaks the unity of the paragraph. A unified paragraph functions like a team where every member (sentence) works toward the same goal (the main idea).

sections.title: Identifying and Fixing Irrelevant Sentences
sections.content: Irrelevant sentences often contain 'true' information that is simply misplaced. For example, a paragraph about a chef's cooking techniques should not suddenly discuss the chef's childhood hobby of stamp collecting. To fix these errors, you have two primary options: 1. Deletion: Remove the sentence entirely if it adds nothing to the main point. 2. Revision: Rewrite the sentence to include a 'link phrase' that explicitly connects the detail back to the main idea.

sections.title: The Unity Test
sections.content: The ultimate test for paragraph focus is the Unity Test: if you remove the sentence in question, does the paragraph become clearer and more focused? If the answer is yes, the sentence was likely a distraction. If the paragraph feels like it has a 'hole' or is missing a logical step, the sentence (or a revised version of it) is necessary for cohesion.

worked_examples.question: Consider this paragraph: 'The city park has become busier over the last decade. Families come on weekends for picnics and children play near the pond. The park's board is considering adding Wi-Fi hotspots so visitors can use their devices while outdoors. Volunteer gardeners meet every Saturday to plant native species. These improvements have increased community use of the park.' Which change to the third sentence best maintains paragraph unity?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the main idea. The paragraph is about 'improvements increasing community use of the park.' Step 2: Evaluate the third sentence. While Wi-Fi is an improvement, the sentence focuses on 'using devices,' which is a tangent. Step 3: Look for a revision that links directly to park usage. A better version would be: 'To support increased visitation, the board plans small improvements like more benches and better signage.' This directly explains why the park is busier and more accessible, maintaining the focus on community use.

common_mistakes: Choosing a sentence just because the information in it is 'interesting' or 'true' even if it doesn't fit the topic.
Failing to identify the main idea before evaluating individual sentences.
Keeping a sentence that introduces a new conflict or sub-topic that the rest of the paragraph does not address.
exam_tips: Always summarize the paragraph in 3-5 words before looking at the answer choices.
Watch out for 'tangent traps'—sentences that start with a relevant word but end on an unrelated topic.
If a question asks if a sentence should be deleted, ask: 'Does this sentence provide a necessary reason, example, or detail for the main idea?'
content.recap: Paragraph unity requires every sentence to support one central idea. Use the Single-Focus Sentence Check to identify tangents, and ensure every detail serves as a reason, example, or explanation for the paragraph's primary theme.

knowledge_claims.content: Paragraph unity is the principle that every sentence within a paragraph must support a single, clearly defined main idea.
The first step in checking for unity is to identify the paragraph's main idea in a single, concise phrase.
A sentence should be removed or rewritten if it does not directly provide a reason, example, or detail that backs the main idea.
The Unity Test involves checking if removing a sentence makes the paragraph's focus clearer; if it does, the sentence likely lacked unity.
Sentences that introduce a new topic or a separate debate, even if factually true, break paragraph unity.
When rewriting a sentence for unity, include a link phrase that explicitly ties the detail back to the paragraph's main idea.
A common mistake is keeping a sentence simply because it contains interesting information, regardless of its relevance to the main point.
A unified paragraph functions as a cohesive unit where every sentence works toward a shared rhetorical goal.
Unlike transitions which link sentences, unity checks ensure the content itself belongs within the specific thematic boundary of the paragraph.
To verify a revision, substitute the new sentence into the paragraph and read it to ensure every sentence now reinforces the main idea.
A 'tangent trap' is a sentence that begins with a relevant keyword but shifts the focus to an unrelated sub-topic.
If a sentence is necessary for the logical flow or provides a required step in an explanation, it should be kept or refined rather than deleted.

videoLesson.title: Revise Paragraph Sentences for Unity
videoLesson.description: Recognize sentences that do not support the paragraph’s single main idea. Name the main idea, then remove or rewrite sentences lacking a clear link.
